headline: Oil turned higher after Iran said the US hit one of its bases, lifting US yields and the dollar. France's unrest kept the euro near its lows, while China's growth beat lifted the Aussie.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: The dollar firmed a little into the close, helped by a weaker euro and by oil turning higher after Iran said the US hit one of its naval bases. US 10-year yields rose to about 5.15%. Builder confidence fell to a 14-year low, but it didn't move the Fed debate.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the morning's calm broke in the afternoon. Iran's navy said two small US projectiles hit its Konarak base, wounding two soldiers; the US has not confirmed it. It is the first such strike in seven weeks, and the Houthis also claimed a run of attacks on Saudi oil sites. Oil swung from a morning loss to a gain, inflation worry came back, and the 10-year yield rose about 6bp to near 5.15%. The dollar index ended near 102, up about 0.15%, mostly because the euro fell. The one US print, the NAHB builder index, ran the four beats: (1) it asks homebuilders how sales and buyer traffic feel; (2) it fell to 29 against 31 expected, the lowest since 2012; (3) with mortgage rates over 7%, high rates are clearly biting housing; (4) for the dollar, it gives the Fed one small reason not to tighten, but it is a mood survey, not hard data, and the dollar didn't react. Fed pricing held: October a hold (about 84%), December a likely hike (about 90%). Fed official Warsh said he won't prejudge October. Thread: the morning edition said the weekend's fears never fired and the dollar would wait on data. The data was quiet; geopolitics came back instead. What it means: the dollar's support today came from others' trouble (France) and from oil pushing yields up, not from new US strength. The lens: are higher oil prices pushing US yields up faster than the Fed debate can?
chapters.fx: What to watch: China's loan rates about 8 PM CT tonight (no change expected); US housing starts and permits 7:30 AM CT Tuesday; pending home sales 9 AM CT; any US word on the Konarak claim. The Fed stays in its quiet period until the October 27–28 meeting.

scenarios.base: If the Konarak claim stays a one-off and US housing data is soft but orderly, the dollar keeps drifting with the euro and with yields.
scenarios.bull: If the US confirms more strikes or oil keeps climbing, yields rise further and the dollar gains on both the haven and the rate channel.
scenarios.bear: If a real US–Iran step toward reopening Hormuz appears, oil and yields fall back and the dollar loses today's lift.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro slid about 0.2% to near $1.121 as France's unrest spread into its bond market. French 10-year yields jumped to near their highest since 2002 and European stocks fell more than 1%. Tomorrow's budget revenue vote in Paris is the next test.
chapters.meaning: What changed: France's trouble moved from the street into markets. The French 10-year yield rose about 9–13bp to roughly 4.9–4.94%; the gap over German bonds hit about 146bp before easing to about 141bp. Every major European stock index fell 1.1–1.6%, and French banks dropped about 3%. The four beats on the spread: (1) the French–German yield gap is the extra pay investors demand to hold French debt; (2) it widened again, and stocks and bonds fell together; (3) that combination signals worry about France's finances, not a normal risk-off day, where bonds usually rally; (4) for the euro, higher French borrowing costs mean less appetite for euro assets, so the euro softens. The euro hit a 16-month low against the pound and a 3-month low against the franc. Commerzbank noted the reaction is milder than early October; the euro stays under real pressure mainly if the tension spreads beyond France. Thread: the morning edition said the euro had found its own negative driver. The afternoon confirmed it. What it means: this is a France story, not a dollar story. The ECB still looks set to hold on October 29 with December the live meeting, but that rate support is being outweighed by fiscal worry. The lens: does Tuesday's vote calm French bonds or push yields higher?
chapters.fx: What to watch: German producer prices 1 AM CT Tuesday; ZEW sentiment 4 AM CT; France's revenue-section budget vote Tuesday; Lagarde speaks Wednesday; Moody's France review Friday.

scenarios.base: If Tuesday's vote passes without big concessions, French yields steady and the euro holds near its lows.
scenarios.bull: If the vote passes cleanly and the protests fade, the spread narrows and the euro recovers some of today's loss.
scenarios.bear: If the vote fails or the unrest spreads beyond France, the spread widens and the euro tests last week's 16-month low.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: The pound slipped about 0.2% against a firmer dollar but hit a 17-month high against the euro as money left France. The real test starts tonight: UK jobs data at 1 AM CT, then inflation on Wednesday, with a November hike almost fully priced.
chapters.meaning: What changed: little UK news, but the euro's weakness made sterling a relative winner. EUR/GBP hit its lowest in 17 months, while GBP/USD eased to about 1.330 as the dollar firmed. Thread: the morning edition said the November hike case had firmed and the question was whether Wednesday's inflation print starts pricing December too. Nothing today changed that. Governor Bailey has said energy costs haven't spread much into wider UK prices yet, but that it is too early to be sure. What it means: the pound is waiting on its own data. Tuesday's wage numbers come first: pay cooling would back Bailey's calmer view, while sticky pay would firm the hike case. Then Wednesday's inflation, expected to rise to about 3.4%, decides whether markets look past November. The lens: does this week's data keep the BoE on course to hike, and beyond?
chapters.fx: What to watch: UK jobs and wages 1 AM CT Tuesday; 10-year gilt auction about 4:30 AM CT; MPC member Greene at noon CT; UK inflation 1 AM CT Wednesday; Bailey speaks Wednesday; the budget on October 28.

scenarios.base: If jobs and inflation land near forecasts, November stays locked in and the pound tracks the dollar into the budget.
scenarios.bull: If wages hold up and inflation runs hotter than 3.4%, markets start pricing a December follow-up and the pound gains.
scenarios.bear: If wages cool and inflation surprises low, the hike case softens and the pound gives back ground.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The yen weakened about 0.3% to near 158.5 per dollar as US yields rose on the oil rebound. Swaps now put only a small chance on an October BoJ hike, with December still the likely meeting. Japan's inflation report on Friday is the next test.
chapters.meaning: What changed: two things. First, higher US yields widened the gap the yen has to fight, so USD/JPY rose about 0.3%. Second, the October hike looks less likely than this morning's read: BBH notes swaps price under a 5% chance for October 30 and about 80% for December. BBH expects Friday's inflation to edge up to about 2.1%, still below the BoJ's own forecast, so the bank has no reason to rush. Thread: the morning edition said Ueda's 'quite close' to 2% firmed December without changing October. December holds; October has faded further. What it means: the yen stays a yield-gap story. Words from the BoJ don't close that gap; higher Japanese rates or lower US yields would. The higher oil goes, the more Japan pays for imports, which adds a small weight. The lens: does Japan's inflation beat the BoJ's own forecast? The 160 level, where Japan has stepped in before, is the line to watch.
chapters.fx: What to watch: Japan trade balance 6:50 PM CT Tuesday; Japan national inflation Friday; BoJ October 29–30 (new forecasts); US 10-year yields; 160 per dollar.
numbers: BoJ Oct 30 hike: under 5% (swaps, BBH); Dec ~80%

scenarios.base: If US yields stay near 5.15%, USD/JPY holds in its range below 160 into Friday's data.
scenarios.bull: If Japan's inflation beats the BoJ's forecast or US yields fall, the gap narrows and the yen firms.
scenarios.bear: If oil and US yields keep rising, the yen weakens toward 160, where intervention risk rises.

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: Two-way day for the franc: it slipped about 0.3% against a firmer dollar but rose to a 3-month high against the euro as money fled France. The Konarak report gave the haven only a small floor.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the franc was pulled two ways. Against the dollar it lost about 0.3% to near 0.827, as US yields rose. Against the euro it gained, reaching a 3-month high, because the franc is where European money goes when France gets shaky. Thread: the morning edition marked the franc quiet, with no Swiss news and the haven bid unused. Today the haven bid showed up, but against the euro, not the dollar. What it means: there is still no Swiss driver. The SNB holds at zero with a December cut possible, so the franc moves on outside fear: France and the Middle East. The lens: is fear rising inside Europe or outside it?
chapters.fx: What to watch: France's budget vote Tuesday; any follow-up to the Konarak claim; the SNB's write-up of its last meeting Thursday.

scenarios.base: If France steadies and the Gulf stays tense but contained, the franc drifts with the dollar.
scenarios.bull: If French stress spreads or the Gulf escalates, haven demand lifts the franc more broadly.
scenarios.bear: If both risks fade, the haven bid drains and talk of an SNB cut weighs on the franc.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Aussie was the day's best major currency, up about 0.5% to near 0.698 after China's growth beat. Rising stocks helped too. The RBA's Kent kept a November hike open but noted the job market is loosening faster than expected.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the overnight China lift held all day instead of fading. China grew 4.5% against 4.4% expected, with shoppers doing the surprising, and the yuan hit its strongest offshore level since mid-2022. A tech-led rebound on Wall Street added risk appetite, and AUD/JPY rose about 0.8%. On the RBA: Kent said rates may not be 'restrictive enough' as the neutral level rises, which keeps a November 2–3 hike on the table (about 1 in 3). He also said the job market is loosening faster than expected, a softer note inside a hawkish message. Thread: the morning edition flagged that hedge funds already lean toward the Aussie. The newest CFTC data shows they trimmed that bet, while real money is strongly against it. What it means: the Aussie had a good day on China and risk mood, but its own rate story waits for the October 28 inflation report. The lens: is China demand enough to carry the Aussie until then?
chapters.fx: What to watch: China loan rates about 8 PM CT tonight; RBA Deputy Governor Hauser 5:30 PM CT Tuesday; New Zealand inflation Wednesday; Australia quarterly inflation October 28; RBA November 2–3.

scenarios.base: If China's loan rates hold and risk mood stays calm, the Aussie keeps most of today's gain into the CPI cluster.
scenarios.bull: If Hauser echoes Kent's hawkish side or risk appetite builds, November pricing firms and the Aussie extends.
scenarios.bear: If stocks turn back down or Gulf risk spikes, the hedge-fund bet unwinds and the Aussie gives back the China gain.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: Canada's inflation came in a touch soft at 3.1%, and the core measures fell below 2%, so an October hike stays unlikely. But consumers now expect more inflation, and oil turned higher, so the loonie still firmed about 0.2% to near 1.411 per dollar.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the settler gave a mild, mixed answer. The four beats: (1) prices were 3.1% higher than a year ago; (2) that was a tenth below the 3.2% forecast, and the core gauges the BoC watches cooled to 1.8% and 1.9%; (3) energy is what keeps the headline above 3%; strip it out and inflation sits around the 2% target and is drifting lower; (4) for the loonie, that takes heat off an October 28 hike. TD now sees the next hike in early 2027. Then the BoC's own surveys pushed the other way. Firms grew less gloomy, few expect a recession, and consumers' five-year inflation expectations jumped to about 3.9% from 3.4%. Most interviews came before the late-August trade-talk collapse, and firms asked afterward were gloomier. Markets kept October as a hold with about one quarter-point hike priced by December. Thread: the morning edition said only a hot print would revive October. It wasn't hot, so October stays about 1 in 4. What it means: today's cooler prices versus the higher prices people expect is the BoC's dilemma. The loonie got help from oil and a softer US dollar elsewhere, not from rate pricing. The lens: does the BoC trust today's cool core or tomorrow's expected prices?
chapters.fx: What to watch: oil into Tuesday's November WTI expiry; US housing data 7:30 AM CT Tuesday; Canada retail sales later this week; BoC decision October 28.

scenarios.base: If oil holds near today's levels, the loonie stays steady while October pricing sits near 1 in 4.
scenarios.bull: If oil keeps rising or the BoC leans on the higher expectations, hike pricing firms and the loonie gains.
scenarios.bear: If oil drops back or the BoC drops its hike talk, the loonie loses its support.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: Quiet for the kiwi, roughly flat near 0.566: China's growth beat helped a little, but there was no New Zealand news. Tomorrow's dairy auction comes first; Wednesday's inflation report decides the October 28 hike-or-hold call.
chapters.meaning: What changed: very little. The kiwi took a small lift from China and the better risk mood, but much less than the Aussie. Thread: the morning edition noted a much wider trade deficit, driven by pricier fuel imports, and a cooler services survey, both small arguments for the RBNZ to hold. Those stand. What it means: the RBNZ's October 28 decision is still a close call between a hike and a hold, and Wednesday's inflation figure (about 3.8% expected) decides it. Hedge funds bet against the kiwi and added to that bet in the latest CFTC data, so a hot print would surprise them. The lens: is New Zealand inflation cooling fast enough for the RBNZ to wait?
chapters.fx: What to watch: Global Dairy Trade auction about 9:50 AM CT Tuesday; New Zealand Q3 inflation 4:45 PM CT Wednesday; RBNZ October 28.
numbers: Sep trade deficit NZ$1.97B vs 0.78B expected

scenarios.base: If dairy prices hold, the kiwi waits for Wednesday near current levels.
scenarios.bull: If inflation runs hot, an October hike gets priced and the kiwi rises against funds' bets.
scenarios.bear: If inflation cools and risk mood sours, the hold case wins and the kiwi slips.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Oil turned around: US crude fell toward $96.50 in the morning on the Russia sanctions waiver, then jumped above $103 after Iran said the US hit one of its bases and the Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi oil sites. The market went back to pricing a supply risk, not a deal.
chapters.meaning: What changed: two forces fought all day. In the morning, the Russia waiver eased one supply squeeze, and US crude fell to about $96.50. In the afternoon, Iran's navy said the US struck its Konarak base, the first such strike in seven weeks; the US has not confirmed it. The Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi Arabia in two days, including an Aramco site at Yanbu, one of the routes that lets Gulf oil avoid Hormuz. US crude ended about 1.8% higher near $103; Brent ended near $109, slightly lower. The front US contract expires Tuesday, which can exaggerate its moves. Gulf flows remain a fraction of normal, about 8.5 million barrels a day against over 20 million a week earlier, per Kpler. Iran's foreign minister, alongside Russia's Lavrov, blamed the US for Hormuz tensions and offered no step toward a deal. Thread: the morning edition said the weekend's fears never fired. By the afternoon, the Gulf risk was back. What it means: pricier oil helps exporters like Canada and costs importers like Japan and the euro area, and it lifts inflation worry and yields. The lens: is the Gulf supply hole shrinking, or only the Russia risk?
chapters.fx: What to watch: any US response to the Konarak claim; more Houthi strikes on Saudi export routes; November WTI expiry Tuesday; API inventories 3:30 PM CT Tuesday; Rubio's India trip and the waiver.
numbers: Gulf flows ~8.5m b/d vs 20m+ a week ago (Kpler)
Hedge-fund oil bets among the weakest since 2015 (CFTC)

scenarios.base: If the Konarak claim stays isolated, oil holds a supply premium with large daily swings.
scenarios.bull: If the US confirms more strikes or the Houthis hit Saudi exports again, the premium grows.
scenarios.bear: If US–Iran talks show a real step or Gulf flows recover, the premium drains quickly.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: Gold slipped about 0.6% to near $4,140 even on a day with more conflict news. Pricier oil lifted US yields, and gold pays no interest. It stays stuck in its $4,100–4,200 range while December rate-hike pricing holds.
chapters.meaning: What changed: gold lost ground in the afternoon. The oil rebound revived inflation worry, the US 10-year yield rose about 6bp, and the dollar firmed. Higher yields make an asset that pays nothing less attractive, and that outweighed the haven pull from the Konarak report. Thread: the morning edition said gold's cap holds unless December pricing cracks or a real escalation arrives. Today brought a small escalation, but the yield channel won. What it means: right now yields drive gold more than fear does. Hedge funds still lean for gold but cut that bet over the past month. The lens: are yields or haven demand driving gold right now?
chapters.fx: What to watch: US yields after Tuesday's housing data; Gulf headlines; December Fed pricing through this week's inflation reports abroad.

scenarios.base: If yields stay near today's level, gold stays in its $4,100–4,200 range.
scenarios.bull: If US yields fall back or the Gulf escalates further, gold tests the top of the range.
scenarios.bear: If oil keeps pushing yields up, gold slides toward the bottom of the range.
